name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,820

clue.text: Child's organiser contains letters about assembly (10)

indicators.note: A box contains what has been put in it, so the letters named next sit inside the word before them.
About turn is the order that faces a soldier the other way, so the word it applies to is written backwards.

blocks.note: a parent is the one who organises a child's day
letters are mail, and MAIL turned round reads the other way

explanation.surface: A schoolchild's planner with letters in it about the morning assembly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assembly' is the school hall at nine o'clock in the surface and the one at Westminster in the answer. 'Letters' means the post rather than the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: An assembly is a body of people gathered to deliberate, and the one that sits to make law is the parliamentary kind.

clue.text: Friend throughout the year (4)

blocks.note: raining throughout the day is raining all day
y is the year on a form or a dated file

explanation.surface: Somebody who stays a friend every month of the year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throughout' asks for the whole of something rather than a passage through it, which is how a preposition turns into three letters. Y for year is the single letter on any form that wants a date.
explanation.definitionFit: An ally is the friend who stands with you in a quarrel, the word used of nations and of people alike.

clue.text: Spooner's noticed stolen goods in case (7)

indicators.note: Spooner was the Oxford don who swapped the opening sounds of two words, so the pair named here trade their first noises.

blocks.note: to notice something is to see it, so noticed is saw, and stolen goods are loot

explanation.surface: Spooner catching sight of a thief's haul packed into a case.
explanation.walkthrough: Trading the s and the l at the front turns two short words into two others, the second one changing its spelling but not its noise. 'Case' is the one heard in court.
explanation.definitionFit: A case is what a lawsuit is called once it reaches court, the two words used interchangeably for the same action.

clue.text: Sortie with no parking, couples cycle (3,6)

indicators.note: No parking says there is none, so the letter that stands for parking is struck out of the word holding it.

blocks.note: couples are pairs, any two things taken together
p is the parking of a road sign and of a car park's big blue board
a trike is the three-wheeled cycle a small child rides

explanation.surface: An outing with nowhere to leave the car, so the couples go by bike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycle' sits at the end of the clue where a shuffling instruction would sit, and is a vehicle instead. 'Sortie' is a day trip in the surface and a combat flight in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A sortie is a single mission flown out against the enemy and back, which is the military word for the raid this names.

clue.text: Stretch of Devon river full of vessels (7)

indicators.note: A cupboard full of something has it within, so the word named next goes inside the letters before it.

blocks.note: the Exe is the Devon river that gives Exeter its name
pans are the vessels standing on a cooker

explanation.surface: A length of a Devon river crowded with boats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessels' are the kitchen kind, not the ones the surface has floating on the water. The Exe is the river most often wanted when Devon is mentioned, and it is three letters long.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretch of moor or of water is an expanse of it, both words meaning an unbroken area you can see across.

clue.text: Body temperature approximately (5)

blocks.note: t is temperature in a formula or across the top of a chart
ten or so means approximately ten

explanation.surface: Taking a rough reading of somebody's body temperature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body temperature' is one idea in the surface and splits across the definition and the first letter of the wordplay. The answer is only the trunk, so 'body' is being used for the part with no head or limbs.
explanation.definitionFit: A torso is the body without head or limbs, the sense in which a sculptor or an anatomist speaks of a body.

clue.text: Strike before 12 breaks record (4)

indicators.note: Whatever breaks into a house ends up inside it, so the letters named before it go into the word named after.

blocks.note: an LP is the twelve-inch vinyl record
am covers the hours before twelve noon

explanation.surface: A walkout starting before noon that beats the previous record.
explanation.walkthrough: '12' looks like a cross-reference to another entry and is the clock face instead, which makes 'before 12' the morning. 'Strike' is the fist, not the picket line.
explanation.definitionFit: To lamp somebody is British slang for hitting them hard, so 'strike' is the verb in its punching sense.

clue.text: Party girl ate nuts (5,2)

indicators.note: Somebody nuts is out of their right mind, and letters out of their right order follow.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: A party girl making a whole meal of a bowl of nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party girl' reads as one phrase, and the first word of it is the definition standing alone. The answer is British slang from the nineties club scene for going out and enjoying yourself loudly.
explanation.definitionFit: To large it is to party hard, the phrase carrying the same boastful swagger as 'party' used as a verb.

clue.text: Watch driver graduate before summer starts (10)

blocks.note: an MA is a Master of Arts, the graduate's two letters
the time before summer starts is spring, so anything then is in spring

explanation.surface: Keeping an eye on a driver who graduated shortly before the summer began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before summer starts' looks like an instruction about a first letter and is a plain statement of the season. 'Watch driver' is the chauffeur being observed in the surface and one machine part in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The mainspring is the coiled spring whose slow unwinding drives a mechanical watch, so it is what makes the watch go.

clue.text: Telephone book diminished (6)

blocks.note: b is the book of a bible or a catalogue reference
to lower a price or a voice is to diminish it

explanation.surface: A telephone directory that has shrunk since the last edition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Telephone book' looks like the directory, and only the first word of it is the definition. Getting on the blower is how a British speaker says picking up the phone.
explanation.definitionFit: The blower is old British slang for the telephone, from the speaking tubes you blew down to get attention.

clue.text: Painter opens wine, just the thing for painting? (8)

indicators.note: To open a thing is to make a gap in the middle of it, and the letters named before it drop into that gap.

blocks.note: port is the fortified wine that goes round the table after dinner
RA is a Royal Academician, the painter elected to London's Royal Academy
just the thing is just it, the very article wanted

explanation.surface: A painter uncorking a bottle, the ideal subject for a picture.
explanation.walkthrough: RA printed after a name on a gallery label means Royal Academician, which is how a painter shrinks to two letters. The question mark admits that only some paintings have a sitter.
explanation.definitionFit: A portrait is a painting of a person, so 'painting' defines it by the wider class it sits in.

clue.text: Old British car gives mojo to spy (6,6)

blocks.note: Austin was the Birmingham marque behind the Seven and the Allegro, dropped by British Leyland in the eighties
whatever powers a thing is what gives it its energy

explanation.surface: A vintage British motor handing its magic over to a secret agent.
explanation.walkthrough: Mojo is the word this particular agent loses in the second film, so the surface has been quietly about him from the start. Austin was a real marque, which is what lets the first half read as scene-setting.
explanation.definitionFit: Austin Powers is the bungling secret agent Mike Myers plays in the film spoofs, so 'spy' names him by example.

clue.text: Madonna beds German philosopher and later Roman general (4,6)

indicators.note: To bed a plant is to set it down inside the soil, so what is named next goes within the word before it.

blocks.note: the Madonna of the altarpieces is the Virgin Mary
Immanuel Kant of Konigsberg wrote the Critique of Pure Reason
later on is on, as in ten years on

explanation.surface: Madonna taking a German philosopher to bed, and a Roman general after him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Madonna' is the singer in the surface and the Virgin in the wordplay, which is what makes the bedding shocking and then harmless. Kant is the German philosopher a puzzle nearly always means.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Antony commanded Caesar's legions and then lost Actium to Octavian, so 'Roman general' is his job stated plainly.

clue.text: Knot steadies New Yorker's hood (4,4)

indicators.note: A knot is a tangle, and a tangled word comes out with its letters in a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A knot holding a New Yorker's hood down in the wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hood' is American for the neighbourhood somebody grew up in, which turns a garment into a district. The Upper and the Lower one are both stretches of Manhattan.
explanation.definitionFit: A New Yorker's hood is the neighbourhood they claim, and the East Side is one of Manhattan's, upper and lower.

clue.text: Firework you shouldn't have inside according to daughter (6)

indicators.note: What is put inside a thing sits among its letters, so the piece named before it goes into the middle of the words after it.

blocks.note: per is according to, as in as per the instructions
d is daughter in a family tree or a Who's Who entry
ta is the British thank-you, and you shouldn't have is what you say over a present

explanation.surface: A banger your daughter says you were wrong to bring into the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You shouldn't have' is the polite protest over a gift, so the thanks hiding behind it are two letters. Hamlet's hoist with his own petard is the bomb-maker blown up by his own device.
explanation.definitionFit: A petard was a small case of gunpowder for blowing in a gate, and the name carried over to the banger sold at firework shops.

clue.text: Tasty drink brought over on a board (9)

indicators.note: A thing brought over is turned over on its way, so the word named is written out backwards.

blocks.note: to lap is to drink the way a dog does, and those letters come back the other way
the clue's own a, taken as it stands
the board of board and lodging is the table you eat at

explanation.surface: A tasty drink carried over to a table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' is the table you take your meals at, the sense kept alive in board and lodging rather than the plank the surface suggests. The drink is a verb here: to lap.
explanation.definitionFit: Palatable food is food the palate is content with, which is a plainer way of saying it tastes good.

clue.text: City spread jokes about Pep's termination (6)

indicators.note: Butter spread across bread goes everywhere at once, so the letters named come out in a new order.
Letters set about a thing close round it, so the single letter named next finishes up among them.
A termination is where something stops, so take the last letter of the word before it.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
the last letter of Pep

explanation.surface: Jokes going round about Pep Guardiola losing the Manchester City job.
explanation.walkthrough: A capital C on 'City' beside Pep points straight at Manchester City's manager, and the definition wants any city at all. 'Termination' is the sack in the surface and a final letter in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Skopje is the capital and much the largest city of North Macedonia, so 'City' defines it by class.

clue.text: Squash blood under shoe (7)

indicators.note: In a downward answer whatever goes under something is written below it, so the word named first is entered second.

blocks.note: a pump is the flat soft shoe worn for dancing or for gym
your own flesh and blood are your kin

explanation.surface: Blood being trodden into the floor under the sole of a shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squash' is the crushing verb in the surface and a family of thick-skinned gourds in the answer, marrows and courgettes among them. Kin is blood relations, the word behind next of kin.
explanation.definitionFit: A pumpkin is a squash, the gourd grown along the ground and hollowed out at Halloween, so the definition names it by kind.

clue.text: Sort of rubber star wears still wet in odd places (8)

indicators.note: You wear a coat round the outside of yourself, so the piece named before it goes inside the letters after it.
The odd places are the first, third, fifth and seventh, so only the letters standing in those positions are kept.

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of STILL WET, counted straight through both words
an icon is a star of screen or stage

explanation.surface: A star of rubber films putting on an outfit that is still damp in patches.
explanation.walkthrough: The odd letters run straight through 'still wet' as though the space were not there, which is what hides them. 'Star' is a person in the surface and the word for one in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Silicone rubber is the heat-proof synthetic used for baking moulds, seals and bathroom sealant, so it is one sort of rubber among many.

clue.text: Old pictures on loan guarded by security service (7)

indicators.note: Somebody guarded by minders has them all round, so the letters named next close over the word before them.

blocks.note: SIS is the Secret Intelligence Service, the proper name of the agency everybody calls MI6
anything out on loan has been lent

explanation.surface: Old paintings out on loan with security keeping watch over them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pictures' is the cinema rather than the gallery, which makes them films from before sound arrived. Britain's foreign intelligence agency signs itself with three letters, not the two-and-a-number of the films.
explanation.definitionFit: The silents are the films made before talkies took over in the late twenties, so 'old pictures' is the cinema's own name for them.

clue.text: Dock where dog follows rat (7)

indicators.note: What follows comes along behind, so the word named before it is written second.

blocks.note: a cur and a rat are both names for a thoroughly nasty man
to dog somebody is to tail them through the streets

explanation.surface: A quayside where a dog goes chasing after a rat.
explanation.walkthrough: Neither animal is an animal: the rat is the man and the dog is the shadowing. Docking is what a vet does to a tail, so the answer takes its own definition apart.
explanation.definitionFit: To dock a speech or a wage is to cut it short, the same thing done to a dog's tail with shears.

clue.text: Presumably all-female cult are changing terminology (12)

indicators.note: What is changing will not stay as it was, so the letters named come out in a different order.

blocks.note: an all-female gathering would presumably have no men in it
the seven letters of CULT ARE changed round

explanation.surface: A cult presumed to be women-only is bringing its terminology up to date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Presumably' does real work: an all-female gathering is one you would guess holds no men, and that guess is the first five letters. 'Changing' reads as the cult modernising its language.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomenclature is the system of names a subject uses for its things, which is what 'terminology' says in plainer words.

clue.text: Governor thanked for hiding PM faced with revolting Americans (5)

indicators.note: Something hiding is there without announcing itself, so the letters run unbroken through the words before it.

blocks.note: the letters run on across the join between the two words

explanation.surface: A governor being thanked for sheltering the prime minister from furious Americans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' is the American Revolution rather than anybody's manners, and the prime minister of those years is the man who lost the colonies. 'Governor' is a job title in the surface and half a hiding place in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord North was prime minister throughout the American War of Independence, so the definition names him by the crisis of his term.

clue.text: Wet seed that's no good (4)

definitions.note: 'Wet' reads as an adjective in the surface while the answer is a noun, but British usage makes the wet a name for the rain itself, as in coming in out of the wet.

indicators.note: No good says there is none, so the letter that stands for good is dropped from the word holding it.

blocks.note: a grain of wheat is the seed the crop grows from
g is good on a school report

explanation.surface: A damp seed that will never come to anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wet' has to be read as a noun, the way a farmer talks about being out in the wet all day. G for good is the letter the clue takes away.
explanation.definitionFit: Rain is what a British speaker means by 'the wet' when complaining about being caught out in it.

clue.text: Spectator's running after large rugby player, having lost his head (6-2)

indicators.note: What comes after a thing is written behind it, so the piece named first is entered last.
A man who has lost his head has lost his top, so the first letter of the word before it goes.

blocks.note: L is the large on a clothing label
the hooker is the forward in the middle of the front row who hooks the ball back in a scrum
the head of the word is its first letter, and it is the one that goes
a machine that is running is on

explanation.surface: A spectator jogging along behind a big rugby forward who has panicked.
explanation.walkthrough: Losing your head is panicking in the surface and losing a first letter in the wordplay. 'Running' is the state of an engine rather than anything the spectator's legs are doing.
explanation.definitionFit: A looker-on is somebody who watches without joining in, which is what a spectator at a match does all afternoon.

clue.text: Spoilt child claims Chad's inside India (6)

indicators.note: A claim takes a thing in and keeps hold of it, so the letters named next sit within the word before them.
The inside of a word is what is left once both its ends are taken off.

blocks.note: a brat is the spoilt child of the family
the middle two letters of CHAD, with the C and the D taken off

explanation.surface: A spoilt child insisting that Chad lies somewhere inside India.
explanation.walkthrough: Chad is an African country in the surface and just a four-letter word to be gutted in the wordplay. Indians call their country this in Hindi, and the constitution gives the two names equal standing.
explanation.definitionFit: Bharat is the Hindi name for India, used on passports and in the constitution alongside the English one.

clue.text: Song that guy heard (4)

indicators.note: What is heard is a noise rather than a spelling, so write down the word that sounds like the one named.

blocks.note: that guy is him, and the two are said exactly alike

explanation.surface: A song that one particular man listened to.
explanation.walkthrough: Four words of clue and two of them are the definition, which leaves almost nothing to go on but the sound. The silent n is what stops the spelling giving it away.
explanation.definitionFit: A hymn is a song of praise sung in church, so 'song' names it by the wider class.

clue.text: How's saving weight significant on a cheap holiday? (10)

definitions.note: The answer is a gerund and the clue defines it by the situation it puts you in — somebody hostelling is somebody on a cheap holiday — with the question mark owning the stretch.

indicators.note: Saving here means except for, the way all saving one does, so the letter named next is left out.

blocks.note: the clue's own first word, its apostrophe ignored
w is weight in a formula or on a luggage label
a telling detail is a significant one

explanation.surface: Wondering whether travelling light matters much when the holiday is a cheap one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saving' is economising in the surface and means except for in the wordplay, which is the one word to watch. Youth hostels have been the cheap bed in Britain since the nineteen-thirties.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody hostelling is touring on the cheap, sleeping in hostel dormitories rather than hotels, which is what a cheap holiday amounts to.
